synopsis: Model risk combines a simulation’s influence on a decision with the consequence of getting that decision wrong, and determines the credibility evidence required; although described as influence multiplied by consequence, it is operationalized as a low/medium/high grid rather than a formula with units [f14567, f7597, f14570]. Across the frameworks reviewed, credibility is conditional on a defined use and operating envelope, with risk-scaled verification, physical-data validation, uncertainty assessment and independent review; the comparisons include ASME V&V 40 (2018), FDA guidance from November 2023, NASA-STD-7009B (2024) and its February 2026 handbook, while NATM evidence is explicitly on-road [f186, f8073, f9454, f9760]. Credibility goals must be agreed before evidence collection, and neither a universal agreement tolerance nor a universal minimum or percentage of physical testing is prescribed [f7642, f7538, f7646, f14577]. For this collision-mitigation program, the physical brake model is judged probably the highest-risk model because of wear, temperature and braking consequences, while sensor models in dust, darkness and glare also carry high risk because validation is weakest there [f14574, f14575]. The resulting planning recommendation is to rate each claim’s risk and retain physical confirmation for high-consequence or weak-model claims; broad procedural scene coverage alone is not adequate if generation rules omit the structures that cause real failures [f14579, f10552, f10990, f3736].
